references.text: Joseph again emphasizes that it is God who gives the interpretation of dreams, when Pharaoh tells him about his dreams.
Joseph tells Pharaoh that God has revealed to him what He is about to do, which reinforces Joseph's conviction that dream interpretation belongs to God.
Daniel praises God because He reveals deep and hidden things and knows what is in the darkness – parallel to Joseph's belief that interpretations belong to God.
Daniel tells King Nebuchadnezzar that it is God in heaven who reveals secrets, parallel to Joseph saying that dream interpretations belong to God.
King Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges that Daniel's God is a God who reveals secrets, after Daniel interprets his dream with God's help.
Direct narrative connection: The prisoner's confession in prison presupposes and leads directly to Pharaoh's acknowledgment of the same inability.
Clear thematic parallel: Both texts challenge the limits of human wisdom by requiring both a dream and its interpretation as proof of divine insight.
Strong theological parallel: Acknowledgment that no human wise men can interpret dreams, but that one man has God's Spirit to do so.
Theological confirmation: Joseph repeats and specifies his statement that the interpretation comes exclusively from God.
